arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: William Lockyer argued the Supreme Court must defer to state court fact-finding in habeas review.
He stated the Ninth Circuit did not simply apply the wrong standard of deference.
Drozdowski argued the Ninth Circuit correctly found the state court's fact determination unreasonable.
He claimed the prosecutor failed to provide a single persuasive reason for striking the juror.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: This case examines the standard of review for state court fact-finding in habeas corpus proceedings. It focuses on the prosecutor's obligation to explain juror strikes.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: the sides that brought the case want the Supreme Court to affirm the state court's deference to the prosecutor's explanation.
the opposing sides want the Supreme Court to uphold the Ninth Circuit's finding that the prosecutor's explanation was insufficient.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: the sides that brought the case argue the Supreme Court must defer to state court fact-finding under federal habeas statutes.
the opposing sides argue the state court unreasonably determined facts because the prosecutor gave no persuasive reason for the strike.

sections.heading: What the justices asked
paragraphs: Chief Justice Roberts asked if the state fact-finder merely gave the benefit of the doubt to the prosecutor.
Justice Souter asked if the district attorney claimed youth alone did not explain the strike because other young jurors remained unchallenged.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: This case defines the minimum explanation a prosecutor must provide when striking a juror. It clarifies how federal courts review state court decisions in habeas proceedings. The outcome shapes the practical application of Batson challenges in criminal trials.
